Benjamin Cox
BEN-juh-min KOKS
n. proper (Particular Baptist minister and confessor; c.1595–c.1663)
Benjamin, from Hebrew Binyamīn (son of the right hand; the favored or fortunate son; Gen 35:18); Cox is an English surname variant of Cock, from Old English coc (cock, cockerel), a medieval byname. Cox was a Particular Baptist minister whose lasting legacy is his Appendix to the 1644 First London Baptist Confession, the earliest full statement of Particular Baptist soteriology attached to that confessional standard.

Biblical Definition

Benjamin Cox (c.1595–c.1663) was a Particular Baptist minister of Bedford and one of the key theological voices of the formative period of Particular Baptist confessionalism. Educated at Oxford and briefly a Church of England clergyman, he encountered Particular Baptist convictions and was baptized upon profession of faith. His most significant contribution was his Appendix to the 1644 First London Baptist Confession, published as a supplement to the second edition (1646). While the Confession itself articulated the ecclesiological and soteriological distinctives of the seven churches, Cox's Appendix addressed the theological implications of Calvinistic soteriology — election, the covenants, and the nature of saving faith — with a systematic clarity that complemented the Confession's more polemical tone. He corresponds to a tradition of Particular Baptist confessionalism that would reach its fullest expression in the 1689 Second London Baptist Confession, which Particular Baptists still hold as their primary subordinate standard. Cox also engaged in correspondence with John Tombes and other baptismal controversialists of the era. His life represents the pattern of a man formed in one tradition (Anglican), convicted by Scripture to a different ecclesiology, and committed enough to the Reformation's doctrinal heritage to anchor his new convictions in written confession — the tool the Reformers themselves had used to guard the faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

Particular Baptist minister and author of the Appendix to the 1644 First London Baptist Confession; Cox's systematic expansion of that Confession's soteriology placed Calvinistic doctrine at the center of early Particular Baptist identity and anticipated the more comprehensive 1689 London Baptist Confession.

COX, Benjamin (c.1595–c.1663). Particular Baptist minister of Bedford; formerly of the Church of England; author of the Appendix to the 1644 First London Baptist Confession (published with the 1646 second edition). His Appendix addressed election, faith, and the covenants with a Calvinistic thoroughness the Confession itself had not spelled out at length.

His Anglican background — Oxford education, clerical orders — meant Cox came to Particular Baptist convictions through studied engagement with Scripture and the Reformed tradition rather than through separatist radicalism. He never abandoned the Reformed doctrinal heritage; he reexpressed it within a Baptist ecclesiology.

The Appendix holds that saving faith is the gift of God to the elect, not the autonomous decision of a free will; that election is unconditional and according to God's sovereign good pleasure; and that the covenant of grace, properly understood, encompasses only those effectually called. These are standard Reformed positions, applied within a believer's-baptism ecclesiology.

Cox engaged John Tombes, the leading anti-paedobaptist scholar of the era who remained paedobaptist in his ecclesiology while denying infant baptism's Scriptural warrant. The Cox-Tombes correspondence and published exchange illustrate the diversity of arguments circulating in mid-seventeenth-century Engish Calvinist circles over baptism.

His place in the genealogy of Particular Baptist confessionalism is clear: the 1644 Confession with Cox's Appendix forms the earliest full-dress statement of Particular Baptist identity; the 1689 Confession, which largely follows Westminster, is the mature form of what Cox's generation began.

Modern Corruption

Revisionist Baptist histories have sometimes portrayed the early Particular Baptists as de facto Arminians or as doctrinally thin; Cox's Appendix refutes this directly: from the beginning, Particular Baptist identity was built on Calvinistic soteriology, not merely on baptismal practice.

expand to see more

Contemporary evangelical Baptists who have drifted toward Arminianism or who treat soteriology as a secondary matter of preference often invoke “Baptist identity” while ignoring that the founding Particular Baptist documents were emphatically Calvinistic. Cox's Appendix is the earliest extended proof: the Particular Baptists did not differ from the Reformed on soteriology; they differed on ecclesiology and baptismal mode. Their confessions explicitly affirmed total depravity, unconditional election, definite atonement, and effectual calling — the same doctrines that structured the Westminster Confession.

Church-growth pragmatists and post-conservative Baptist theologians have used “Baptist freedom” to detach Baptist churches from the Confession tradition altogether, treating any written standard as a threat to individual conscience. Cox and his generation understood the opposite: a clear written confession is the instrument by which a church guards the gospel entrusted to it against drift and corruption. Baptist freedom means freedom from human traditions, not freedom from Scripture's dogmatic content.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Cox's confessional work grew from Oxford Anglican education, Reformed soteriology, and the Particular Baptist fellowship of mid-seventeenth-century Bedford; his Appendix became the first published extension of Particular Baptist doctrinal self-understanding beyond ecclesiology.

expand to see more

Oxford University — Cox's Anglican education grounded him in the Reformed scholarship of the English church and gave him the theological tools to argue his Baptist convictions in learned terms, not merely popular ones.

1644 First London Confession — the foundational Particular Baptist confessional document; Cox's Appendix (1646) expanded its doctrinal scope into soteriology, covenantal theology, and the nature of saving faith.

Bedford Particular Baptist fellowship — Cox served a congregation in Bedford, the same region that would later nurture John Bunyan; the Bedford circle represented the heartland of English Calvinist Dissent.

John Tombes controversy — Tombes' learned anti-paedobaptism was conducted from a position that denied baptismal regeneration without endorsing immersion; Cox's exchange with Tombes sharpened the theological case for Particular Baptist polity.

1689 London Baptist Confession genealogy — the line from Cox's Appendix (1646) to the 1677/1689 Confession represents a continuous effort of Particular Baptist confessional development, moving from a seven-church polemical document to a full-dress Westminster-parallel standard.

Usage

"Cox's Appendix is essential reading for any Particular Baptist who wants to understand where their tradition came from: from the beginning, the Particular Baptists were Calvinists who happened to be Baptists, not Baptists who happened to be Calvinists."

"The existence of Cox's careful confessional writing in the 1640s refutes the claim that Baptist identity was formed in opposition to confessionalism; the Particular Baptists built confessions as eagerly as the Presbyterians because they shared the Reformers' conviction that clear doctrine is the guardian of a living church."

"Pastors teaching the history of Reformed Baptist thought should begin with Cox's Appendix as the bridge between the Elizabethan Puritan heritage and the mature 1689 Confession, showing that Particular Baptist soteriology was inherited from the Reformed tradition, not invented by Baptists."
